reference: Elish, M. C. (2019). Moral crumple zones: Cautionary tales in human-robot interaction. Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, 5, 40-60.
note: Supports the claim that responsibility migrates to the nearest human operator who had limited control, quoted from the Abstract and the Introduction; limitation: a qualitative comparative case study that diagnoses misattribution but supplies no normative rule for correct allocation, and the supplied PDF text layer carries no page numerals, so it is cited by section only.

reference: Johnson, D. G. (2020). Engineering ethics: Contemporary and enduring debates. Yale University Press.
note: Supports the rotten-apples-and-rotten-barrels reading of mishaps and the separation of accountability, blameworthiness and liability, quoted at p. 118 and from the section Sorting Out Responsibility; limitation: only the page numerals 118 and 119 survive in the supplied file, so the later passages are section-anchored, and the chapter is a case synthesis rather than an argument about AI.

reference: Luegenbiehl, H. C., & Clancy, R. F. (2017). Global engineering ethics. Butterworth-Heinemann.
note: Supports the anti-scapegoating thesis, that converging causal conditions make it unfair to place all responsibility on single actors, quoted at pp. 84, 86 and 87; limitation: the available pages concern Hurricane Katrina rather than AI or medicine, and the thesis can immunise organisations against accountability if read too strongly.

reference: Matthias, A. (2004). The responsibility gap: Ascribing responsibility for the actions of learning automata. Ethics and Information Technology, 6(3), 175-183.
note: Supports the founding claim that learning automata make future behaviour unpredictable and that reduced control reduces responsibility, quoted from the Abstract and the Introduction; limitation: the supplied PDF has no page numerals so it is cited by section, S6 holds that it covers only the culpability gap, and its own lung-cancer example concedes that blame is possible where limitations were known beforehand.

reference: Reijers, W., Young, M. T., & Coeckelbergh, M. (2025). Introduction to the ethics of emerging technologies. Palgrave Macmillan.
note: Supports the claim that responsibility presupposes capacity and institutional support and that innovation outruns regulation, quoted at pp. 85 and 86; limitation: an introductory chapter that asserts the gap at the level of innovation governance and offers no operational criterion for who must verify post-deployment performance.

reference: Santoni de Sio, F., & Mecacci, G. (2021). Four responsibility gaps with artificial intelligence: Why they matter and how to address them. Philosophy & Technology, 34, 1057-1084.
note: Supports the four-way taxonomy of culpability, moral accountability, public accountability and active responsibility, and the many-hands point, quoted at pp. 1059, 1065, 1066, 1073 and 1077; limitation: a conceptual framework that assumes the gap it taxonomises and presents meaningful human control as programmatic future work, which is exactly what S8 rejects.

reference: Santoni de Sio, F., & van den Hoven, J. (2018). Meaningful human control over autonomous systems: A philosophical account. Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 5, Article 15.
note: Supports the requirement that supervision be real rather than nominal, through the tracking and tracing conditions, quoted from the Abstract and the section Meaningful Human Control: Tracking and Tracing; limitation: the journal uses article locators and the PDF has no page numerals, the account originates in lethal autonomous weapons and is extended to civil systems only programmatically, and traceability to a human does not by itself establish that the human could act.

reference: Tigard, D. W. (2021). There is no techno-responsibility gap. Philosophy & Technology, 34, 589-607.
note: Supports the counter-argument that a technology-specific responsibility gap is a prevailing assumption rather than a demonstrated fact, quoted from the Abstract and section 1 Introduction; limitation: the supplied file retains only the page numeral 590 so it is cited by section, the author sets legal liability aside, and he analyses ascription to agents without offering a design or institutional criterion, so he does not reach active-responsibility or public-accountability gaps.

reference: van de Poel, I., & Royakkers, L. (2011). Ethics, technology, and engineering: An introduction. Wiley-Blackwell.
note: Supports the four conditions of blameworthiness, the demanding foreseeability standard and the treatment of a failure to act as causal contribution, quoted at pp. 9 and 12; limitation: the supplied PDF contains chapter 1 only, so the whitelist pages 252-267 are absent and this source is not used for the hierarchy and organization or forward-looking models, and the book is an introductory text oriented to individual agents.

reference: Young, I. M. (2006). Responsibility and global justice: A social connection model. Social Philosophy and Policy, 23(1), 102-130.
note: Supports the shared and forward-looking social connection model and the five features that distinguish it from the liability model, quoted at p. 103; limitation: the model was built for global labour justice, it supplements rather than replaces the liability model, and it deliberately declines to isolate perpetrators, which limits what it can ground for a licensed medical device.
